messages.subject: Discrete-time, multi-state CJS model with uneven time intervals
messages.subject_clean: Discrete-time, multi-state CJS model with uneven time intervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

I’m working on a discrete-time multi-state extension of the Cormack-Jolly-Seber
survival model, similar to examples in Ch. 9 of Kéry and Schaub 2012. However,
the time intervals of surveys are not evenly spaced. Surveys were conducted at
approximately 6-month time intervals but can vary from 5 to 7 months. To account for this I’ve made a simple adjustment using exponentiation of each survival
parameter (phi[i,t], where i is an individual and t is a time step) by the
number of months (months[t]) between surveys for each time interval, for
example phi[i,t]^months[t], thereby obtaining monthly survival estimates (attached ...-months.R).

Does this seem like a reasonable approach to deal with uneven
time intervals? Are there pitfalls to using this approach? The results appear similar when I derive survival parameters
for 6 months compared to the model that does not account for the length of time
intervals. I am looking to avoid continuous-time survival models for now.

Thanks in advance for any insights,

Brian

messages.subject: sCJS with unsuitable habitat delineated?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I've previously used the spatially-explicit CJS modeling framework introduced by Schaub & Royle (2014), and I'm interested in revisiting the possibility of modeling information about habitat suitability to constrain potential dispersal locations. I would probably want to simply denote "suitable" vs "unsuitable" areas (grid cells), but I imagine some study systems would benefit from modeling habitat selection probabilities instead.

Schaub & Royle touch on this idea as a potential extension of their model, but I haven't seen it implemented in the sCJS literature. Has anyone here been working on something like that? I'm also not up on the SCR literature - perhaps there's something relevant there?

I'd appreciate any thoughts you might have. Thanks!

Emily Weiser
Emily.L...@gmail.com

messages.subject: Re: Exactly the same results in different runs of multi-species occupancy dynamic model
messages.subject_clean: Exactly the same results in different runs of multi-species occupancy dynamic model
messages.body_plain:
A while ago (July 2018) I noticed some unexpected behavior when using jagsUI.  When I ran update() on a model fit with the jags() function, and then reran the same thing, I got output that was exactly the same as the first time. I expected that I would get different results, due to the random nature of the MCMC sampling. I emailed Ken kellner the author of jagsUI and he wrote back:

Eric,

 An update on this after looking at it in depth:

The ultimate reason for this unexpected behavior is due to the way JAGS generates initial values.

JAGS (and JAGS called from within R by any package, as far as I can tell) does not use the current state of the R random seed when generating initial values.

Instead by default it does so as a function of the system time, outside R.

My approach to running JAGS in parallel in R is to create several completely independent cores and run a single JAGS chain in each core.

Unfortunately, when you do this, each core's JAGS instance is independent and doesn't know about the other parallel instances.

The result is an identical random seed is used by JAGS in each of these independent instances, and you'll end up with completely identical chains (ie the traceplots overlap perfectly).

When not in parallel, JAGS is aware of how many chains you have and thus knows not to do this.

You'd think that if you stagger the start time of these separate instances of JAGS, that might be a way to force them to use different seeds, but I haven't been able to get that to happen.

Thus, the only way to get actual independent chains in parallel is to provide each chain at initialization with a specific (unique, random) starting seed, which is how jagsUI has worked up to this point.

The possibly frustrating result of this is that JAGS saves and continues to use this seed even when updating an existing model, thus creating the perfectly reproducible behavior you see.

So the behavior of each chain is random, it's just that the random seed is fixed when the model is initialized (the same way you'd make an R analysis reproducible using set.seed(123) or similar).

Once I've manually given JAGS a random seed, I can't take it away or change it, or at least I haven't found a way.

So it's a choice between completely identical chains or completely "reproducible" chains in parallel, with the first option obviously being useless.

Until your email, I didn't realize that the reproducibility extended into updates, which is not ideal. I unfortunately don't see an easy fix to this, but will continue to work on it.

In the meantime, I don't think there's anything wrong with the output you get from running in parallel, except in the specific case where you need separate independent update tracks from the same source model fit - if you disagree, I'd be happy to hear your thoughts.

I really appreciate you bringing this to my attention, and hopefully the package is still useful to you!

Ken

messages.body_plain:
I have some questions about modeling of the correlation between occupancy and detectability in the context of community occupancy models. Previously, I've always modeled the correlation (roughly) as follows (i indexes species):

rho ~ dunif(-1, 1)
lpsi.intercept[i] ~ dnorm(beta0.mu <http://beta0.mu>, pow(sigma.beta0, -2))
lp.intercept[i] ~ dnorm(zeta0.mu <http://zeta0.mu> + (rho*sigma.zeta0 / sigma.beta0) * (beta0[i] - beta0.mu <http://beta0.mu>), pow(sigma.zeta0, -2)/(1 - pow(rho, 2)))

Lately, however, I am running multi-scale community occupancy models, where I am modeling occupancy at two spatial scales (corresponding with nested sampling units of survey points nested within 1-km^2 grid cells) along with detectability, which makes me want to take the mutlivariate normal approach using a Wishart prior exemplified in Chapter 11.6.2, Volume 1 of AHM, so that I can model all three pair-wise correlations between coarse-scale occupancy, fine-scale occupancy, and detectability. I have three questions arising for me that I'm hoping someone here can help me answer:

###########
# Question 1 #
###########

I am having trouble understanding the prior for the bi-variate species-specific random effect in chapter 11.6.2. The variance-covariance matrix is implemented as

Omega[1:2, 1:2] ~ dwish(R[,], df)
Sigma[1:2,1:2] <- inverse(Omega[,])
for(k in 1:nspec){ # Group lpsi and lp together in array eta
lpsi[k] <- eta[k,1]
lp[k] <- eta[k,2]
eta[k, 1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu.eta[], Omega[,])
}

For the above, R is given in the data as `matrix(c(5,0,0,1), ncol=2)` and df = 3. Is there an explanation somewhere in the book or that someone can provide here for the values for R and df in this example?

##########
# Question 2 #
##########

I followed a tutorial for psychology researchers, and came up with the approach in the attached file for modeling cross-scale correlations, but looking at the example in AHM, I'm not sure I am doing this right (seems like I am setting priors in too many places). Would it be possible to get a second set of eyes on my code to check if what I am doing is correct?

###########
# Question 3 #
###########

It has always been my understanding that we expect a positive correlation between occupancy and detectability. I've always used an uninformative prior for rho (dunif[-1,1]), but lately I've been wondering if it might make more sense to force rho to be positive (dunif[0,1]). Has anyone considered doing this? Are there any drawbacks that might not be immediately obvious?

messages.subject: HDS with continuous data
messages.body_plain:
I want to share a version of Hierarchical distance sampling (HDS) using continuous data I worked out. To solve the problem of drawing distances for the unobserved (augmented) individuals, which must come from the triangular distribution of probability for a circular area, I used an inverse probability transform. I reasoned that by transforming the CDF of distances F(x)=integral{B^2/distance^2} to it's inverse F.inv(x) = B*sqrt(distance), the distances were mapped onto a uniform distribution (B is the maximum distance observed).  To implement in the model, we must first transform the observed distance onto this inverse probability scale using: distance.transformed = distance.raw^2/B^2. Then to pick a new distance from the correct distribution, we draw from a uniform(0,1) and then transform the distances back to the raw scale using distance.raw = B*sqrt(

distance.transformed). For convenience I kept the observed and unknown (augmented) distances together, but they could be separated if desired. Then only the new distances would need the transformation and the observed distance could be kept on the raw scale in the data input. Attached is an example of this implementation based on example code from "Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology" by Marc Kery & J. Andy Royle, section 8.5.2.

I did some more exploring. Using the code pasted below, I tried different values for R and df to understand their implications for the priors for rho and variance of occupancy and detectability. Based on my explorations, I am thinking that  R <- matrix(c(5, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1), ncol = 3) and df = 4 would be roughly analogous to the R used for the single-scale community model in AHM. It seems like the larger value for R[1,1] sets the prior for occupancy (or large-scale occupancy in the multi-scale model) to be somewhat narrower than priors for small-scale occupancy and detectability, which I suppose makes sense since there are less data at the highest level. It seems to me that setting R[1,1] to 1 would be more uninformative than the R[1,1] = 5 used in AHM, but I like the idea of using weakly informative priors, so I'll follow AHM's lead and set R = matrix(c(5, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1), ncol = 3) for my multi-scale model. Not sure if this in fact constitutes a weakly informative prior, but it seems like it follows the idea of R = matrix(c(5, 0, 0, 1), ncol = 2) for the single-scale model in AHM. Would much appreciate any thoughts or suggestions from the community on this or questions in my initial post. I am still curious what folks think about forcing rho to be positive, but it doesn't seem like there is an easy way to do that with the Wishart prior, so I'll leave that idea aside for now.

library(matlib)

# 2-dimensional (single-scale occupancy)
nsims <- 10000
R <- matrix(c(5, 0, 0, 1), ncol = 2)
df <- 3
Omega <- rWishart(n = nsims, df, R)
Sigma <- Omega
for(i in 1:dim(Omega)[3]) Sigma[,,i] <- inv(Omega[,,i])
rho <- numeric(length = nsims)
for(i in 1:nsims) rho[i] <- Sigma[1, 2, i] / sqrt(Sigma[1,1,i] * Sigma[2,2,i])
hist(rho)
hist(Sigma[1,1,])
hist(Sigma[2,2,])

# 3-dimensional (multi-scale occupancy)
nsims <- 10000
R <- matrix(c(5, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1), ncol = 3)
df <- 4
Omega <- rWishart(n = nsims, df, R)
Sigma <- Omega
for(i in 1:dim(Omega)[3]) Sigma[,,i] <- inv(Omega[,,i])
rho.12 <- rho.23 <- rho.13 <- numeric(length = nsims)
for(i in 1:nsims) {
  rho.12[i] <- Sigma[1, 2, i] / sqrt(Sigma[1,1,i] * Sigma[2,2,i])
  rho.23[i] <- Sigma[2, 3, i] / sqrt(Sigma[2,2,i] * Sigma[3,3,i])
  rho.13[i] <- Sigma[1, 3, i] / sqrt(Sigma[1,1,i] * Sigma[3,3,i])
}
hist(rho.12)
hist(rho.23)
hist(rho.13)
hist(Sigma[1,1,])
min(Sigma[1,1,])
max(Sigma[1,1,])
hist(Sigma[2,2,])
min(Sigma[2,2,])
max(Sigma[2,2,])

messages.body_plain:
Hi Quresh,

I wouldn't use the inverse Wishart. It has a number of fairly well documented problems. See this link for a really fantastic write up of different approaches by Alvarez et al.:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1408.4050.pdf

You might check out the 'dmnorm.vcov' distribution in JAGS. It allows users to define independent priors on the covariance matrix components (sigma's and rho's), and uses a likelihood based constraint to ignore non-positive definite (i.e., impossible) matrices. It's ad hoc, but pretty brilliant. Plummer also implemented a scaled inverse Wishart (JAGS 4.3 user manual) that kind of 'softens' some of the issues caused by the inverse Wishart. Fay and colleagues published a really nice paper recently where they demonstrate the use of a Cholesky decomposition (code is provided in the appendix).
https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1111/2041-210X.13728
If you're starting to use Nimble you can use the Barnard et al. (2000, Statistica Sinica) variance decomposition approach (it can't be implemented in JAGS or BUGS). This allows for specifying independent priors on the variances, and vague priors for the correlations. I think this is probably the best solution.

Anyway, lots of options out there. I think the Barnard approach is 'best' (that's what we use for current projects), but if you want a quick(er) fix then perhaps check out some of Fay et al.'s code or just use dmnorm.vcov() and provide priors for the covariance matrix components. It's tricky to figure out optimal priors with covariance matrices, and then transforming everything with link functions makes it even more complicated. Best of luck!

Thomas

Hi Jordan,

The immediate problem is an error in your data:
jagsData$y[27,1]   # 12
jagsData$z[27,1]   # 1, so that's not the issue
jagsData$nOcc[27]  # 11 (!)

So at site #27 the camera trap was active for 11 occasions, and on 12 occasions it detected CA.Agouti. Does not compute. The error probably arose when you pooled the data into 7-day occasions; that throws away information, and I've never seen a convincing argument in favor of it.

The way you handle the categorical variable trail is suboptimal; in the JAGS code you appear to treat it as a continuous covariate. It's binary, so could be represented at 0/1, off/on trail; in that case the JAGS code would be correct -- the intercept corresponds to off-trail traps and the aTrail coefficient to the difference (on the logit scale) between the on-trail and off-trail traps.

I've no idea what your effort covariate could be. For camera traps, that's usually the number of occasions that the camera trap was operational, and that's correctly included in the model with dbin(..., nOcc[i]).  p is the probability of detecting the species (given it is present) on one occasion at one camera trap and is the same for all occasions; what "effort" would affect that?

Regards, Mike

Hi all,

As a brief follow-up, see the attached script for some different ways to parameterize correlation and covariance matrices in MCMC samplers. This is by no means exhaustive, and apologies it's a simple R script and not more fully commented or 'marked down,' but this may be helpful to folks that are using these approaches in their analyses. Approaches covered include:

1) inverse Wishart (not recommended)
2) scaled inverse Wishart
3) Martyn Plummer's dmnorm.vcov 'trick', highly useful
4) Chen and Dunson 2003 and Kinney and Dunson 2008 (from the excellent write-up in Fay et al.)
5) my best attempt at an LKJ prior in JAGS (note that this is much more straightforward in Nimble or Stan, examples linked)
6) the full Barnard et al. (2000) decomposition approach in Nimble

No promises that this is 'error-free' (particularly the LKJ approach in JAGS). I'm happy to answer questions off-list if folks have any, feel free to make corrections on-list if there are any major errors. Just wish I'd had something like this when I was banging my head against my desk five years ago thinking about these issues with CMR data, and figured I'd blast this out there.

Thomas

Thanks Thomas! It is definitely most helpful to have all of those options in one place.

I have certainly not tried them all, but I did try incorporating the dmnorm.vcov trick into the multi-scale community occupancy context (see attached JAGS code). I tried both an unconstrained version of the model, wherein I estimated all three correlations between coarse-scale occupancy, fine-scale occupancy, and detectability, and a constrained version where I fixed the correlation between grid-scale occupancy and detectability to zero. In both cases, all correlations are estimated to be near zero while both logit grid-scale occupancy (BETA0) and logit point-scale occupancy (beta0) are estimated to be extremely high. In contrast, the old way of specifying two bivariate correlations (commented out in JAGS code and labeled "old way") produces estimates that make a lot more sense, with species-specific estimates more variable and also much more sensible (not shown in the attached summary).

My suspicion is that the bivariate correlation approach is also more directional, i.e., only lower level parameters are subjected to the correlation parameter (e.g, fine-scale occupancy is a function of the correlation between fine-scale and coarse-scale occupancy, but coarse-scale occupancy is only explicitly governed by the community mean and SD). The inverse Wishart approach also did not work (see my original post). I'd be curious to know if any of the other approaches listed by Thomas work better, but my suspicion at this point is that estimating a full correlation matrix with all three correlations is too unconstrained in a multiscale community occupancy context. I am going to revert to the bivariate approach since that has been working fine thus far. I'd appreciate any thoughts or experiences suggesting a multivariate approach that actually works and is better than the bivariate approach. Also, there is certainly the possibility that I made an error in how I implemented the dmnorm.vcov, so I'd appreciate any suggestions on error-correcting adjustments to my JAGS code.

Quresh

Hi all,

I came across this post which greatly piqued my interest as I'm actually attempting to do something similar with my research, but with a multi-species occupancy model, and I'm trying to figure out how to best specify this in JAGS.

For my own research I am interested in examining whether there is a threshold between percent forest cover and mammal species richness in my study area, across sites with varying levels of forest cover, specifically to see if there is a threshold point where species richness steeply declines once the level of forest cover in a given site hits below a particular point. I'll attach my code below where I attempt to specify where/how I might specify the threshold point in the likelihood, but I'm not sure if this is correct, and where else I might need to specify the threshold throughout the model as it's a multi-species model.

Also, since richness is a derived quantity from these models, I'm curious as to whether it makes sense to specify the threshold within the multi-species occupancy model, or doing a secondary analysis in a piecewise/break point regression model (by using the segmented package for example) using the richness outputs across sites and the % forest cover covariates to look for a forest cover threshold would be a better/more straight forward option to examine this?

Any input on this would be greatly appreciated, thank you!

Best,,

Jordan

On Monday, March 21, 2022 at 12:26:33 AM UTC-5 Mike Meredith wrote:
> Hi Jordan,
>
> The immediate problem is an error in your data:
> jagsData$y[27,1]   # 12
> jagsData$z[27,1]   # 1, so that's not the issue
> jagsData$nOcc[27]  # 11 (!)
>
> So at site #27 the camera trap was active for 11 occasions, and on 12 occasions it detected CA.Agouti. Does not compute. The error probably arose when you pooled the data into 7-day occasions; that throws away information, and I've never seen a convincing argument in favor of it.
>
> The way you handle the categorical variable trail is suboptimal; in the JAGS code you appear to treat it as a continuous covariate. It's binary, so could be represented at 0/1, off/on trail; in that case the JAGS code would be correct -- the intercept corresponds to off-trail traps and the aTrail coefficient to the difference (on the logit scale) between the on-trail and off-trail traps.
>
> I've no idea what your effort covariate could be. For camera traps, that's usually the number of occasions that the camera trap was operational, and that's correctly included in the model with dbin(..., nOcc[i]).  p is the probability of detecting the species (given it is present) on one occasion at one camera trap and is the same for all occasions; what "effort" would affect that?
